planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly into saturated, mineral-rich soil so winter cold and moisture break dormancy naturally, or set out nursery-grown plugs in spring; this small tufted sedge needs permanently wet, alkaline ground and will not persist in ordinary garden soil.

directions: Fen star sedge is a diminutive, densely tufted sedge confined to calcareous fens and cold, mineral-charged seeps, where its narrow grass-like foliage and inconspicuous early-summer spikes blend quietly into the surrounding sedge mat. In the Ozark Highlands it occupies the same spring-fed, constantly saturated, lime-influenced muck that supports grass-of-parnassus and other fen rarities, and it struggles anywhere the ground is allowed to dry. Because intact fen habitat is scarce and slow to recover from disturbance, use only nursery-propagated seed or divisions, siting the plant in a continuously wet, alkaline bog garden or spring-fed swale rather than a conventional border. Established clumps spread slowly by short rhizomes and require no fertilizing, only unbroken moisture year-round.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed directly onto saturated, calcareous soil to allow natural winter stratification, or install potted divisions in spring along a spring branch or fen margin; keep the root zone wet and alkaline at all times.

directions: Fen panicled sedge forms substantial, arching clumps considerably taller than most fen sedges, sending up slender triangular stems topped with branched, drooping flower clusters in early summer. It is a clump-forming cool-season sedge of calcareous fens, spring seeps, and marshy meadow edges, actively rooting and spreading in the cool, wet weeks of spring and fall rather than through the heat of summer. In a cultivated setting it works well along the saturated margin of a lime-fed pond or rain garden, where its height and texture provide useful contrast to shorter fen wildflowers without the aggressive spread of many wetland grasses. Divide congested clumps in early spring if flowering declines, and never let the planting site dry between rains.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto exposed, saturated mineral soil for winter stratification, or plant divisions in spring; this fine-textured clumping sedge tolerates more shade than many fen associates but still demands constant moisture.

directions: Prairie star sedge is a slender, clump-forming sedge of calcareous fens, spring seeps, and shaded wet meadow margins, more tolerant of overhead shade than most of its fen-dwelling relatives, which lets it colonize the damp fringe where seep water meets shrub thickets. In Ozark seeps it grows alongside wetland sedges and rushes on a short, star-shaped cluster of flower spikes held just above the narrow foliage in early summer. It performs best in a lime-rich, constantly saturated planting pocket at the edge of a spring-fed water feature, filling in as a textural groundcover without becoming weedy. Leave the previous season's foliage in place over winter and only tidy the clump in early spring once new growth resumes.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed onto wet, loamy or mucky soil for winter stratification; stiff cowbane establishes slowly from a fleshy, fibrous-rooted crown and resents being moved once settled, so choose a permanently damp planting site from the start.

directions: Stiff cowbane is a tall, upright member of the carrot family that haunts wet sand prairies, marsh edges, and the spring-fed seeps and fens of the Ozark Highlands, pushing up rigid, sparsely branched stems topped by flat clusters of small white flowers in late summer when little else is blooming in the seep. Its foliage and roots carry the same toxic compounds found in other Oxypolis and water-hemlock relatives, making it unsuitable near grazing livestock, but it is harmless to handle and valuable as a late-season nectar source for wasps, flies, and small beetles, and as a larval host for black swallowtail caterpillars. Site it in a permanently wet, humus-rich spot such as a rain garden low point or the saturated fringe of a pond, where it needs no staking despite its height. Once established it persists for years without division or fertilizing.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed onto saturated, calcareous soil for natural stratification, or plant divisions or potted stock in spring; despite the common name this is not an invasive purple loosestrife relative but a true Lysimachia confined to high-quality calcareous wetlands.

directions: Prairie loosestrife is a slender, rhizomatous wildflower restricted to undisturbed, mineral-rich wetlands, including the calcareous fens and spring seeps of the Ozark Highlands, where it threads narrow, needle-like leaves along wiry stems that rise from the sedge mat. Five-petaled, bright yellow flowers open along the upper stem in mid-to-late summer and are of particular value to small native bees that specialize on Lysimachia pollen. Because it occurs naturally only where groundwater keeps the root zone cold, wet, and alkaline year-round, it needs the same conditions in cultivation: a spring-fed bog garden, fen restoration planting, or the permanently saturated edge of a limestone-influenced water feature. It spreads modestly by shallow rhizomes once established but is never aggressive, making it a safe companion for other fen specialists.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly where plants are to grow, since the thick taproot resents transplanting once established; cold, moist winter conditions trigger spring germination in wet, mineral-rich meadow or fen soil.

directions: Prairie Indian plantain is a distinctive composite of calcareous wet prairies, fens, and seep meadows, named for its smooth, glossy, plantain-like basal leaves rather than any culinary use. In early summer it sends up a sturdy, unbranched stem topped with a flattened cluster of small, dull white, vanilla-scented flower heads that are consistently worked by small bees, wasps, and beetles, and the hollow stem is a useful field mark distinguishing it from the taller pale and great Indian plantains it is often found growing beside. Its thick taproot anchors it in saturated, mineral-rich soil in the Ozark fens and wet prairie swales where it naturally occurs, and transplanting mature plants is rarely successful, so it is best direct-seeded or set out as a young plug. Once established in a permanently moist, full-sun planting it requires essentially no maintenance and resists deer browsing.
